q: A wine list's 'anchor pricing' works by:
accept: expensive items make neighbors look reasonable
ans: High-priced anchors resetting guests' reference points, making mid-tier bottles feel safe
exp: The second-cheapest-wine effect is its famous cousin.

q: A Negroni pours 1 oz gin ($22/L), 1 oz Campari ($25/L) and 1 oz sweet vermouth ($12/L). At a $16 price, what is the pour cost %?
exp: Batching three-bottle classics is the margin engine of aperitivo hour.

q: Keg wine's business case rests on (name two):
accept: zero bottle waste consistent freshness lower packaging cost pour speed
zero oxidation waste lower cost per pour
less waste and lower cost per pour
zero oxidation and lower cost per pour
ans: Zero oxidation waste on BTG, lower packaging/cost per pour, speed and sustainability
exp: 19.5L keg = 26 bottles; the math sells itself for busy BTG slots.

q: When costing a comped bottle for a VIP table, the accounting hit lands as:
accept: promo expense at cost not lost revenue
ans: A promotional/marketing expense at COST (not menu price) — budgeted, logged, and attributed
exp: Untracked comps become 'variance'; tracked comps become guests for life.

q: The wine director's par level for a BTG pour selling 3 bottles nightly, with weekly deliveries and safety stock:
exp: Par = velocity × lead time + buffer; stock-outs on a listed BTG are unforgivable.

q: Before any small-producer credit, the US federal excise tax on still wine of 16% ABV or less is:
exp: $1.07 per wine gallon, roughly 21 cents a bottle. $1.57 covers wine over 16% up to 21% — so most Port and Sherry — $3.15 covers 21–24%, and $3.40 is sparkling wine. The 2017 Craft Beverage Modernization Act, made permanent in 2020, folded 14–16% ABV wine down into the $1.07 band and added producer credits. That is why fortified wine and Champagne carry a visibly heavier tax line than a 15% Zinfandel, and why the tax bands should shape a direct-import calculation before you quote a price.

q: 'Prime cost', the figure an operator watches hardest, is:
opts: Cost of goods sold plus total labour cost
Food and beverage cost plus occupancy
Gross sales minus cost of goods sold
exp: COGS plus all labour, taxes and benefits included — usually targeted at 55–65% of sales, higher in fine dining. It is the portion of the P&L a manager can actually move week to week; rent, insurance and debt service are fixed. A wine director's decisions land in both halves of it, which is exactly why an ROI argument for another somm has to be made in prime-cost terms rather than in wine-cost terms alone.

q: You are quoted €7.00 FOB per bottle by a Portuguese estate for a direct import. Name the cost layers standing between that quote and your shelf cost.
accept: freight insurance duty federal excise broker fees warehousing state taxes and a wholesaler margin
ocean freight duty excise customs broker storage and the distributor markup
shipping duty excise fees warehousing plus the middle tier of three tier
ans: Ocean freight and reefer container charges, marine insurance, US customs duty, federal excise tax, harbour maintenance and merchandise processing fees, customs broker and ISF filing, drayage and bonded or temperature-controlled warehousing, state excise and licence costs, the exchange rate at settlement — and, in most states, a wholesaler's mark-up, because the wine must still pass through a licensed distributor
exp: The FOB price is the smallest surprise in the stack, and it is landed cost — not FOB — that you divide by your target cost percentage. The line candidates forget is the last one: unless you hold your own importer and wholesaler permits, three-tier does not vanish because you paid the producer directly, and the middle-tier margin is a cost you cannot design away.

q: A guest correctly rejects a bottle as corked. Walk through the financial handling.
accept: replace it log the bottle and claim credit from the distributor
open a new bottle keep the faulty one for supplier credit
replace and return the bottle for credit ringing it as spoilage not a comp
ans: Replace it from stock immediately and re-present, then retain the faulty bottle with its cork and capsule and log it. Most distributors credit or replace confirmed corked bottles under their defect policy, usually requiring the bottle back and sometimes within a stated window, so the loss is recovered at cost rather than absorbed. Ring the replacement in the POS as spoilage or breakage, not as a comp and not as a void, so inventory reconciles and the bottle does not resurface later as unexplained variance
exp: The service cost of a corked bottle is one pour; the accounting cost is zero if the paperwork is done and the full retail margin if it is not. Untracked defects are among the quietest contributors to a bad variance number, and a programme with no spoilage line in its POS is a programme that cannot tell theft from TCA.

q: Your distributor offers to pay for printing your new wine list and to throw in two free cases. Which federal law does that run into, and what are the consequences?
accept: the faa act tied house provisions enforced by the ttb
federal alcohol administration act trade practice rules on tied house
tied house and commercial bribery rules under the faa act
ans: The Federal Alcohol Administration Act's trade-practice provisions — the tied-house and commercial-bribery rules at 27 CFR Parts 6 and 10 — enforced by the TTB, plus state versions that are frequently stricter. Free goods, paying a retailer's expenses and any 'thing of value' furnished to induce purchase are unlawful inducements. Both parties are exposed: the supplier or wholesaler faces TTB penalties or action against its basic permit, and the licensee faces state fines or licence suspension
exp: The lawful versions are the ones the regulations carve out: post-offs and depletion allowances offered on the same terms to all accounts, permitted samples within stated limits, and staff education. A useful working test — if the offer would embarrass you when a competing account learned of it, it is probably an inducement rather than a programme.

q: An invoice for $9,000 is offered at 2/10 net 30. What do you save by paying early, and what is that worth annualised?
accept: save $180 which is worth around 36 to 37 percent a year
two percent is 180 dollars roughly 37% annual return
ans: $180 saved — 2% of $9,000 — for paying twenty days early, an effective annual return of roughly 37%
exp: The arithmetic is 2/98 × 365/20 ≈ 37%. No cellar investment and no allocation returns anything near that, so a solvent programme takes every cash discount offered. When a business starts skipping them, that is a cash-flow warning to read carefully — not a purchasing decision.

q: Name the To Kalon vineyard's original 1868 planter.
exp: Oakville's crown jewel; Mondavi, Opus One, MacDonald and Beckstoffer farm pieces — the name itself has been litigated.

q: 'Rutherford dust' describes the tannin signature of which bench's Cabernets?
ans: The Rutherford bench (alluvial fans west of Hwy 29)
exp: André Tchelistcheff's phrase; BV and Inglenook built its legend.

q: Which mountain AVA east of the valley floor produces Dunn's famously unyielding Cabernets?
exp: Above the fog line: volcanic ash and tuff, small berries, iron tannin.

q: Match Napa AVA to its character.
ans: Stags Leap–velvet · Calistoga–heat · Carneros–cool · Spring Mtn–west slopes
exp: Stags Leap's palisades radiate afternoon heat but the bay breeze slips in by evening.

q: The 1976 Judgment of Paris red winner was made by which winemaker at Stag's Leap Wine Cellars?
exp: A Chicago liberal-arts lecturer turned cellar hand; the bottle sits in the Smithsonian.
